catalog_quote: The vowels /æ/ and /ǝ/ are identified as “weak” and the others as “strong,” based on a number of distinctions, most notably that /æ, ǝ/ cannot receive the word-level accent (which is always root-initial, and realized as a louder and longer vowel). However all seven vowels can appear in roots, monosyllabic or otherwise. /ǝ/ is deleted word-finally if it has the same tone as the preceding vowel, and /æ/ cannot appear word-finally, with very few exceptions. ... Konyagi has high, low, falling, and rising tones. Noun class prefixes are unspecified for tone, being low when the noun is spoken in isolation.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Wamey is a two-tone (H/L, with HL and LH contours) language that, according to Santos 1996 as reported by Merrill, also has a non-contrastive word-level accent fixed on the root-initial (stem-initial) syllable, i.e. the first syllable after any noun-class or infinitive prefix; it is realised as greater loudness and length. The weak vowels /æ, ə/ are said not to carry it.
new_statements.exceptions: Weak vowels /æ, ə/ cannot bear the accent (how root-initial weak-vowel roots such as /sǽt/ 'blood', /lə̀n/ 'snake' are accented is not explained in the second-hand reports); prefixes are outside the accent domain. Corpus-medial contour tones and floating-H docking (Rolle & Merrill 2022) concern tone, not accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent counted from the root/stem left edge (noun-class prefixes excluded); described from citation forms in Santos' grammar of the central (fæ̀gæ̀ntə́) prestige dialect. Statement is Merrill's one-sentence summary of Santos 1996, not an independent analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same language, wame1240 (names: Wamey, wæ̀-mèỹ, Mey, Wèy/W̃eỹ, Konyagi, Koñagi, Coniagui). Santos 1996 (the primary behind Merrill's and Rolle & Merrill's statements) describes chiefly the central prestige dialect (fæ̀gæ̀ntə́) of the Koundara plain, Guinea, with only minor phonetic differences reported for the northern (wə-xàỹə́) and southern (wæ-gə̀ɗ) dialects; Glottolog lists no sub-dialect codes.
